name: Coronary arteries
func: The arteries that feed the heart muscle itself. They branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve and wrap around the heart, delivering the oxygen and fuel it needs to keep beating.

levels.kid:
Your heart pumps blood to your whole body, but the heart is a muscle too, and it gets hungry! It needs its own blood supply.

The **coronary arteries** are the heart's own special food tubes. They start right at the beginning of the body's biggest blood tube, the aorta, and wrap around the outside of the heart like a crown. ("Corona" means crown.)

There's a right one and a left one, and they split into smaller and smaller branches that dive into the heart muscle. If one of these tubes gets blocked, part of the heart can't get oxygen and gets hurt. That's what a heart attack is.
levels.hs:
The two **coronary arteries** arise from the **aortic sinuses** just above the aortic valve and run in the grooves on the heart's surface, cushioned by fat.

The **left coronary artery (left main)** is short. It passes behind the pulmonary trunk and splits into two. The **left anterior descending (LAD)** artery, running down the front groove between the ventricles toward the apex, supplying the front of the left ventricle and most of the septum. The **circumflex artery**, curving left and around the back in the groove between the left atrium and ventricle.

The **right coronary artery (RCA)** runs in the right atrioventricular groove around to the back of the heart. It usually supplies the right ventricle and, in most people, the **SA node** and **AV node**.

The artery that gives off the **posterior descending artery (PDA)** decides "**dominance**." In about 70–80% of people it's the RCA (**right dominant**).

Used blood drains back through **cardiac veins** into the **coronary sinus**, which empties into the right atrium. The LAD is sometimes nicknamed the "widow-maker" because a blockage near its start damages so much muscle.
levels.college:
Branches worth knowing. The **LAD** gives **diagonal branches** to the anterolateral LV wall and **septal perforators** that supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum, including the **bundle branches**. The **circumflex** gives **obtuse marginal** branches to the lateral wall; in left-dominant hearts (about 10%) it gives the PDA. The **RCA** gives the **conus branch**, the **SA nodal artery** (from the RCA in about 60% of people), **acute marginal** branches to the RV, the **AV nodal artery** (from the dominant artery, usually the RCA) and usually the PDA. About 10% are **co-dominant**.

Coronary flow is unusual: in the **left ventricle**, most flow occurs during **diastole**, because systolic contraction squeezes the intramyocardial vessels shut. The RV, with lower wall pressure, is perfused in both phases. So a fast heart rate, which shortens diastole, reduces LV perfusion time.

The heart extracts about 70–75% of the oxygen from coronary blood even at rest, far more than most organs. It therefore can't extract much more when demand rises; it must **increase flow**, via **metabolic autoregulation** (adenosine, nitric oxide, potassium channels opening with low oxygen).

The coronary arteries are **functional end arteries**: collateral connections exist but are usually too small to save muscle when a major branch is suddenly blocked.
levels.phd:
**Atherosclerosis** begins with endothelial dysfunction at sites of disturbed flow (branch points, inner curvatures). **LDL** particles enter the intima and become oxidized; endothelial cells express adhesion molecules such as **VCAM-1**, recruiting monocytes that become macrophages and engulf lipid via scavenger receptors, forming **foam cells**. Smooth muscle cells migrate in and build a **fibrous cap** over a **necrotic lipid core**.

Most heart attacks are caused not by the tightest plaques but by **vulnerable plaques**: thin fibrous caps (under about 65 µm), large lipid cores and heavy macrophage infiltration. Macrophage **matrix metalloproteinases** weaken the cap; when it **ruptures** (or the surface **erodes**), exposed tissue factor and collagen trigger platelet aggregation and thrombus, abruptly occluding the vessel.

Inflammation is causal, not just a bystander: the **CANTOS** trial showed that blocking interleukin-1β reduced cardiovascular events without lowering cholesterol. **Clonal hematopoiesis** (CHIP), in which mutated blood stem cells such as those with TET2 mutations expand with age, raises coronary risk by producing more inflammatory macrophages.

Ischemia progresses as a **wavefront**, from subendocardium to epicardium, over hours: hence "time is muscle." Myocytes stop contracting within about a minute and die after roughly 20–40 minutes of complete occlusion. Paradoxically, restoring flow causes **reperfusion injury** through calcium overload, reactive oxygen species and opening of the **mitochondrial permeability transition pore**, an active target in research.
levels.expert:
**Acute coronary syndrome** presents with crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm or jaw, sweating and nausea; women, older people and people with diabetes often have atypical symptoms. **High-sensitivity troponin** rises with myocardial injury.

The ECG localizes the culprit artery: ST elevation in **V1–V4** = LAD (anterior); **I, aVL, V5–V6** = circumflex (lateral); **II, III, aVF** = usually RCA (inferior). An inferior MI can cause **bradycardia and heart block** (AV nodal artery) and **RV infarction** with low blood pressure. **Wellens' pattern** (deep T-wave inversion in V2–V3) warns of a critical proximal LAD stenosis.

**Coronary angiography** is the gold standard, often combined with pressure-wire testing (**FFR**). **CT coronary angiography** rules out disease in lower-risk patients.

Other causes: **spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD)**, coronary vasospasm, embolism, **Kawasaki disease** in children (coronary aneurysms), and **anomalous origin** of a coronary artery running between the aorta and pulmonary trunk, a cause of sudden death in young athletes.

Treatment in general terms: emergency reopening with **percutaneous coronary intervention (stents)** for ST-elevation MI, antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, statins, and **coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)** for complex multi-vessel or left main disease, using the internal thoracic artery and saphenous vein as conduits. Dual antiplatelet therapy after stenting becomes a real issue if the patient later needs urgent neurosurgery, because of bleeding risk.

keyPoints: Arise from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve
Left main → LAD + circumflex; right coronary artery (RCA)
The artery giving the PDA defines dominance (RCA in ~70–80%)
LV is perfused mainly in diastole
Blocked artery → myocardial infarction; ECG leads localize it
Treated with stents (PCI) or bypass surgery (CABG)

test.q: Which artery runs down the front of the heart between the ventricles?
test.explain: The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex.

test.q: When does most blood flow into the left ventricle's muscle?
test.explain: Systolic contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels, so LV perfusion is mainly diastolic.

test.q: 'Dominance' is defined by which artery gives off the posterior ______ artery.
test.explain: Whichever artery supplies the PDA (usually the RCA) is called dominant.

test.q: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF most likely points to blockage of the:
test.explain: Inferior leads usually reflect RCA territory (in right-dominant hearts).

test.q: Used blood from the heart muscle drains into the right atrium via the coronary ______.
test.explain: Cardiac veins converge on the coronary sinus in the posterior AV groove.
